Article Title: In 2022 US Department of Agriculture funded a trial by spreading cardboard in gardens to avoid weeds; by the second season weeds covered only 15% of the cardboard beds compared to 45% in tilted beds
Article Text:
Cardboard blocks light from reaching the weeds

Not all that good?

Weeds can destroy 50% to 90% of a field's crop yield if left entirely uncontrolled, according to data from the Weed Science Society of America (WSSA) and US Department of Agriculture (USDA). In order to reduce the amount of weeds growing in fields, the USDA in 2022 funded a trial by spreading cardboard beds in gardens. By the end of the second season, weeds covered 15% of the soil in the cardboard beds, whereas 45% of the soil in the tilled beds was covered, according to the project's final report.The trial was funded by USDA's Western SARE program , with the University of Wyoming as a partner and aimed to cultivate the crops without tilling. In the spring of the year, the team conducted the trial at Sweet Hollow Farm, a horticultural farm in Idaho. They covered four raised beds, each about 30 meters long, with cardboard and compost and tilled another four, using the same cardboard-in-the-garden technique that many hobbyists use every fall."If it works, this system could be important for small producers," farmer Jonah Sloven told Western SARE in 2022.At the Sweet Hollow Farms, the problem was bindweed, a climbing plant that spreads by seed and horizontal roots. "Even with spring tillage, we spend a lot of time hand-weeding throughout the season to control bindweed," Sloven said, and that's why he did the math: "Reducing weed pressure cuts working hours, lowers costs, and improves the quality of life for farmers."In the second year, it took two people an average of 55 minutes to weed the raised beds with cardboard and two hours for the tilled ones. The farmers noted in the report that "weeding the raised beds with cardboard was much more pleasant, because the weeds came out with much less effort," and almost no bindweed appeared, except in the holes they dug to take samples.Harvest results were mixed. In 2022, kabocha squash yielded 28% more in raised beds and spaghetti squash 40% more when grown on cardboard, but five delicata squash plants had to be replaced because they didn't grow through the cardboard. In 2023, the four varieties of onion and shallot produced more when grown on cardboard, between 3% and 97% more.The technique is called sheet mulching, where the soil is covered with cardboard or thick paper and organic matter is then added in a layer on top. A July 2025 guide from Oregon State University states that this barrier suffocates weeds and seeds in the soil, "denying them access to the sunlight they need for photosynthesis and growth."With perennials, things change. The Oregon guide recommends pulling up blackberries, bindweed, or couch grass first, because layered or lasagna composting "may not smother these weeds," and advises overlapping the edges by at least 20 centimetres, because "weeds will find any gap, wherever it is and however small it may be."Iowa State University estimates that it takes numerous months to completely kill the plants underneath and thus it is better to start in the fall to plant in the spring. "Fall is an excellent time because the material decomposes slowly over the winter and is ready for planting in the spring," said the guide by Oregon.A 2019 study from Washington State University made a serious concerns about the method. Khurram Shahzad and Markus Flury’s team filled test containers in a greenhouse with soil and compost, covered them with wood chips, cardboard, weed barrier fabric, or plastic, and left others with bare soil for comparison. For 16 days, they measured carbon dioxide and oxygen at depths of 6.5 and 13.5 centimetres because, as Chalker-Scott explained, the soil contains organisms—"from microbes to earthworms, moles, and roots"—that use that oxygen, and "anything that interferes with that exchange is going to be detrimental to the health and life of the soil. ""A single sheet of cardboard was ten times worse than ten centimetres of wood chips," said horticulturist Linda Chalker-Scott one of the study authors in a talk for the International Society of Arboriculture in 2023.Thus, it is better to work with one of two layers of cardboard and not more. The Oregon guide suggested brown corrugated cardboard, without gloss or printing, with all tapes and staples removed and thoroughly soaked before covering. It then recommends adding three to four inches of leaves or compost on top.Once the vegetation has died underneath, Iowa advises removing or tearing up the cardboard so it doesn't hinder new plants, because if it remains, "soil health can also be compromised."
Article Summary: USDA funded a trial by spreading cardboard beds in gardens. By the end of the second season, weeds covered 15% of the soil in the cardboard beds. In 2022, kabocha squash yielded 28% more in raised beds and spaghetti squash 40% more.

Article Title: ‘We’re going to the Moon to stay’: Jeff Bezos targets a sustainable lunar base after investing $28 billion in Blue Origin since 2000
Article Text:
Jeff Bezos reveals why the 1969 moon landing cost the US billions

Why repeating a historic moon landing is not a simple task

Bezos outlines vision for long-term lunar exploration

The moon could provide resources for future space travel

Bezos reveals $28 billion investment in Blue Origin since 2000

More than 50 years after the first crewed moon landing, Jeff Bezos has a straightforward explanation for why returning to the lunar surface remains so difficult. The Amazon founder says the United States devoted almost 3% of its gross domestic product (GDP) to the effort in 1969, making Apollo an exceptionally expensive national project. During an October 2026 interview with Fox News presenter Bret Baier, Bezos argued that the next phase of exploration must take a different approach. He tentatively identified December 2026 as the month for a lunar mission later this year. Rather than sending astronauts on brief visits, he wants to build a sustainable lunar base, backed by billions of dollars in investment through his space company, Blue Origin.Bezos's explanation centres on the financial commitment behind the original moon landing. Speaking to Baier, he recalled that the United States devoted almost 3% of its GDP to the effort in 1969. The figure, he argued, helps explain why the achievement cannot simply be repeated by recreating the technology used during the Apollo missions.The Apollo programme was a national undertaking shaped by the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. Following Soviet successes in the early space race, including the launch of Sputnik in 1957, Washington treated reaching the moon as a strategic priority.As reported by Nasa, President John F. Kennedy set the goal of landing a man on the lunar surface and returning him safely to Earth in 1961. The commitment brought together government funding, scientific research, industrial manufacturing and thousands of workers across the country.Apollo 11 fulfilled that ambition on 20 July 1969, when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to walk on the moon. Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard the command module.Bezos's remarks address a distinction that can be overlooked when looking back at the landing. The United States had the capacity to undertake the mission, but it also had to sustain the political and financial commitment needed to make it happen.The Apollo missions were conducted under circumstances that differ considerably from those facing space agencies and private companies today. During the 1960s, the prospect of beating the Soviet Union to the moon gave the American government a compelling reason to direct vast resources towards a clearly defined objective. That level of spending was possible because lunar exploration had become a matter of national prestige and geopolitical competition.The passage of time has not removed those engineering difficulties. Nor does the existence of modern computing, improved materials and more advanced manufacturing automatically make every aspect of spaceflight cheaper. New systems still need to be tested, and human missions require additional safeguards that uncrewed flights do not.The question raised during the Fox News interview therefore goes beyond the original Apollo achievement. It concerns how to make lunar travel repeatable, affordable and useful over a longer period, rather than treating each expedition as a rare event supported by an exceptional burst of public spending.Bezos has described a future in which astronauts do more than land on the moon, conduct experiments and return home. His stated ambition is to establish a sustainable lunar base, creating infrastructure that could support continued scientific work and further exploration.Such a settlement would represent a different kind of commitment from the Apollo programme. The earlier missions were designed around specific objectives, with astronauts spending limited periods on the surface before returning to Earth. A permanent or regularly occupied facility would require a much broader range of capabilities, including reliable transport, power supplies, communications, equipment maintenance and systems to support human life.Bezos told Baier, “Today, we’re going to do it at a lower cost and going to the Moon to stay.”“It won’t be just a mission and leave. It will be a real sustainable Lunar Base.”During the interview, Bezos also described the moon as a useful destination because of its relatively short distance from Earth. A journey takes roughly three days under typical mission conditions, although the precise travel time depends on the spacecraft and trajectory.He sees the lunar environment as a possible source of materials and ‘interesting things’ that could eventually support activities beyond the moon itself. Among the possibilities he discussed were producing solar cells and rocket propellant using resources available in space.Bezos has also argued that developing the moon should come before sending humans to Mars. A lunar programme could provide experience in operating away from Earth, although the moon and Mars present different environments and logistical challenges. For now, the proposed use of lunar resources remains part of a longer-term vision rather than an established commercial system.The scale of Bezos's ambition is reflected in his personal investment in Blue Origin. According to his October interview with Fox News, he has put $28 billion into the company since founding it in 2000. The business has spent years developing launch vehicles, engines and other technologies intended to support commercial spaceflight and more ambitious missions. Blue Origin's activities extend beyond the goal of establishing a lunar base. Bezos said, “We just raised $10 billion from outside parties for the first time.”“Some day Blue Origin will have an IPO.” Bezos suggested that investors should not expect it to happen immediately. He did not provide a precise time, saying it could be ‘several years away’.A public listing would give outside investors an opportunity to buy shares in the business, while potentially providing the company with another route to raise capital. It would also bring greater scrutiny of its financial performance, development costs and commercial prospects.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos says the 1969 moon landing cost the US billions. The Amazon founder says the next phase of exploration must take a different approach. He wants to build a sustainable lunar base, backed by billions of dollars in investment through his space company, Blue Origin. He tentatively identified December 2026 as the month for a lunar mission later this year.

Article Title: A street vendor turned selling baklava outside concerts into a business that hit nearly $70,000 in monthly sales
Article Text:
Representative Image of selling baklava to enthusiastic fans at a lively concert ( AI Generrated Image)

Jacob Komarow, known as Roy Donk: how a concert-side experiment became Good Baklava

Turkish baklava, pop-ups, wholesale orders and online sales

What the $70,000 peak and $20,000 monthly average reveal about sales

In September 2021, Jacob Komarow impulsively bought 3 trays of baklava on his way to a Phish concert in California, intending to resell them to fellow fans. When a friend doubted he could sell all 3 trays, Komarow bet that he could. The experiment became the starting point for Good Baklava, a business that now sells Turkish pastries through street sales, pop-ups, wholesale orders and online purchases. Komarow, who uses the name Roy Donk, has become known in New York City as the “Baklava Guy”. According to CNBC, Good Baklava averaged just over $20,000 in monthly sales over a recent 9-month period. Entrepreneur reported that sales came close to $70,000 in December 2025, the business’s best month to date. These figures represent sales, not profit, and do not establish how much the business earns after expenses.Komarow’s first attempt to sell baklava began as a challenge involving a Phish concert in 2021. As reported by Entrepreneur, he bought 3 trays from a Middle Eastern grocery store and set out to sell them to concertgoers. He ultimately sold the trays at a profit, tripling his initial investment. For almost 3 years, he treated baklava sales as a concert side hustle before expanding to other outdoor events and pursuing the business full-time.Komarow operates under the name Roy Donk, a reference to the comedy series I Think You Should Leave. Reporting by Resident has connected the name to the character, while coverage by The New York Times has featured the street-selling phenomenon around New York City.In June 2026, Komarow handed out free baklava to Knicks fans outside Madison Square Garden, an appearance that helped his videos gain attention online, according to Entrepreneur. CNBC has also reported on his sales to strangers in local parks and his distribution of free pastries after Knicks games. These activities have contributed to his public profile, but the available reporting does not establish how much each appearance contributed to the company’s revenue. A June 2026 profile in The New York Times brought further attention to the business. Entrepreneur reported that Good Baklava had worked with US Mobile, Acme Smoked Fish and local and national restaurants. The available information does not establish that these partnerships began as a result of the newspaper profile. The account of the partnerships is based on the founder’s comments and media reporting rather than an independently measured assessment of the profile’s commercial impact.Good Baklava sources its pastries from a supplier in Gaziantep, Turkey, according to Entrepreneur. The company’s website describes the product as sourced in Türkiye and explains that its trays are frozen for transport before being baked in New Jersey. The website also identifies Turkish pistachios among the product’s ingredients. The business sells through several channels, including street sales, temporary stands, pop-ups, wholesale orders and its online shop. CNBC’s reported monthly average covers multiple sales channels rather than online and in-person purchases alone.Good Baklava’s website offers several pack sizes, Turkish delights and branded merchandise. It also advertises group-gifting options and free shipping on orders above $100. At the time of checking, the company listed its 12-piece pack for $29.99, its 20-piece pack for $44, its 36-piece pack for $69.99 and its 72-piece pack for $136. These are the prices displayed on the company’s website and may change. Entrepreneur, citing CNBC, reported that 3 pieces sold in person for $10 to $15.Good Baklava’s reported sales have varied considerably from month to month. Entrepreneur reported that the business generated close to $70,000 in sales in December 2025, its best month to date, helped by holiday orders. Sales fell to less than $10,000 the following month. CNBC reported average monthly sales of just over $20,000 across a recent 9-month period. The average and the December peak describe different aspects of the business: one reflects sales across several months, while the other represents an unusually strong month. Neither figure should be interpreted as the founder’s personal income or the company’s profit.Revenue also does not account for the costs of running the business. These may include production, ingredients, transport, packaging, labour and expenses associated with selling at events. Without verified figures for costs and net earnings, the reported sales figures cannot establish the company’s profitability. Good Baklava began with a small experiment selling pastries to concertgoers and developed into a business with multiple sales channels and a growing public profile. Its reported figures show both a strong sales peak and a sharp decline the following month. The distinction between sales and profit remains essential when assessing the business’s financial performance.
Article Summary: Good Baklava sells Turkish pastries through street sales, pop-ups, wholesale orders and online purchases. Founder Jacob Komarow bought 3 trays of baklava on his way to a Phish concert in California in September 2021. He ultimately sold the trays at a profit, tripling his initial investment. For almost 3 years, he treated bak lava sales as a concert side hustle before expanding to other outdoor events.

Article Title: Oscar Whitfield wins 2026 Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year title with close-up image of a dung beetle in Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park, along with five other stunning pictures
Article Text:
Pic credit: Oscar Whitfield

Labour of Love

Pic credit: Oscar Whitfield

More winning photographs

The Aftermath

Pic credit: Federico Veronesi

Photographer: Federico Veronesi, Italy

Category: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026

Location: Huab River Valley, Namibia

Flight of the Bumblebee

Pic credit: Amelie Davis

Photographer: Amelie Davis, UK

Category: 10 Years and Under

Location: Surrey, England

The Meeting Place

Pic credit: James Lewin

Photographer: James Lewin, UK

Category: Animals in their Environment

Location: Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya

Birdsong Painted in Light

Pic credit: Konrad Gräeter

Photographer: Konrad Gräeter, Germany

Category: 15–17 Years

Location: Baden-Württemberg, Germany

Shifting Sand

Pic credit: Sitaram Raul

Photographer: Sitaram Raul, India

Category: Behaviour: Invertebrates

Location: Thar Desert, Rajasthan, India

Oscar Whitfield was on a family game drive in Zimbabwe when he saw a dung beetle struggling up a patch of sand. The beetle was pushing a ball of dung uphill, with a line of flies following behind. This moment caught Whitfield’s eye. He was only 14 at the time. He captured the rare moment. Titled ‘Labour of Love’, the photograph earned the British photographer the Young Grand Title at the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.Oscar Whitfield, who lives near Victoria Falls, spotted the dung beetle while on a family game drive in Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park. He wanted to capture the moment in all its glory. So, instead of standing over the beetle to take the picture, he lay down in the dust. His camera sat at the same height as the insect. He tried different angles and compositions before settling on one. The result was simply perfect. The black-and-white photograph captured how hard the beetle works at a job that looks simple from above. “I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world,” Whitfield said after winning the Young Grand Title, the BBC reported.From a bumblebee captured mid-flight to a blackbird singing at dawn, this year’s winning photographs celebrate the beauty and diversity of the natural world, capturing extraordinary moments that often go unnoticed. Take a look at the winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026.Italian photographer Federico Veronesi won the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 title for capturing a ‘heartbreakingly poignant’ image of a female elephant carrying a dead calf through Namibia’s Huab River Valley. “Of all the 20 years I’ve spent photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrenching, fascinating and dramatic,” Veronesi said. He described the photograph as “revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals”.According to Kathy Moran, chair of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year jury, the winning photograph “says it all”. “This photograph works on so many levels. Emotionally, it’s a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually, it’s proof that animals have cognition.”Amelie Davis, who is in the 10 Years and Under category, took her winning photograph in her garden in Surrey, England, using her dad’s smartphone. She proved that a perfect photograph does not need a plane ticket or fancy cameras. The picture freezes one wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it gets ready to land on a flower. The bee looks almost still, which is the point. The moment lasts only a fraction of a second.James Lewin captured the animals in their habitat. His black-and-white photograph shows a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole. He used an infrared-converted camera to soften the harsh light and create a dreamlike effect.Konrad Gräeter went to a vineyard in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, at sunrise. Spring is when male blackbirds climb to high places and sing to attract a mate. Dawn is when they sing their most complicated songs, and Gräeter was there to capture the moment.Sitaram Raul spent his nights in India’s Thar Desert looking for scorpions. He saw many of them hunting in the dark. Once the sun came up and the temperature climbed, the scorpions had to get out of the heat. This one dug into the shifting sand, and Raul caught it halfway through the process. A perfect moment!Meanwhile, the exhibition opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday, 16 October 2026.
Article Summary: Oscar Whitfield, 14, won the Young Grand Title at the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition. Italian photographer Federico Veronesi won the title for a photograph of a female elephant carrying a dead calf through Namibia’s Huab River Valley. Amelie Davis, who is in the 10 Years and Under category, took her winning photograph in her garden in Surrey, England.

Article Title: In 2020, Olivia Culpo launched More Than a Mask to fight pandemic hunger; her initiative went on to fund over 3 million meals through Feeding America, according to her 2025 Hall of Fame profile
Article Text:
How Olivia Culpo launched More Than a Mask

Partnership with Express

How her family influenced her philanthropy

The COVID-19 pandemic deepened food insecurity across the US, with Feeding America estimating that 45 million people, including 15 million children, could face hunger in 2020. Against this backdrop, model and entrepreneur Olivia Culpo launched More Than a Mask in May 2020, selling fashion face coverings to raise funds for hunger relief. The initiative later funded more than 3 million meals through Feeding America, according to Culpo’s 2025 Rhode Island Heritage Hall of Fame profile.Back in 2020, Culpo celebrated her 28th birthday by announcing the launch of the initiative in partnership with Reunited Clothing. She launched a line of non-surgical, non-medical masks whose sales would be used as charitable donations to various charities. The masks, available in animal prints, satin fabrics and even denim, were priced at $20 and could be purchased online at morethanamask.org.In May 2020, the month's sales benefited Feeding America, where each mask sold provided 100 meals to those in need. "Ever since our local health officials mandated mask-wearing, I thought to myself, how can I do something innovative while providing help to those around me Welcome to more than a mask! Did you know before the COVID-19 pandemic struck, 1 in 7 people in the U.S.were struggling with hunger. Today, school closures mean that 22 million children who rely on school meals have an additional barrier to accessing food. Our community needs us now more than ever. I created this organisation in hopes to get food access to those directly in need," she wrote in a post on Instagram at the time.Later she collaborated with new styles in partnership with Express called #ExpressTogether.For every Express Together face covering sold, a donation of $10 was made to Feeding America through August 2020. “I knew Express would be able to provide way more meals and we would enjoy working with each other as we did before,” Culpo said to WWD at the time. “When you see someone that’s wearing a face mask or a covering of any kind, you know they’re trying to do their part in some way. What we should all be doing right now is coming together and doing the best that we can for everyone.”By 2021, Culpo's initiative was able to provide over 1.5 million meals. “As soon as the pandemic hit, it was pretty much second nature for me to figure out something to do because I felt horrible. I felt guilty. I was depressed for others, but also felt really depressed because I knew how fortunate I was and that made me feel really bad. So I channelled that and really asked myself how I could make a difference,” she said to Modern Luxury in 2021. Rather than letting the guilt remain, Culpo decided to turn it into a practical response to raise awareness and make impact.The initiative later expanded its charitable partnerships. More Than Mask collaborated with other charity organisations such as Colour of Change which is a racial justice organisation, and PERIOD, which eradicated period poverty and supports menstrual health awareness, to target other issues and help out those in need.In a 2021 interview with Shape, Culpo credited her parents for her passion for philanthropy. "My mom and my dad always had such an open-door policy. They would take people in all the time," she said. "I remember my mom, ever since we were little, would 'adopt' families and we would buy all their Christmas presents. And we'll go to soup kitchens and we'll help serve the community. My parents made it second nature to me: If you have enough to give, you have to give it. "Throughout her time in the limelight, Culpo has supported several charitable causes. During her pageant years as Miss USA and Miss Universe, she advocated for breast cancer, ovarian cancer and AIDS/HIV awareness, and has continued working with amfAR to raise awareness and funds for AIDS research and prevention. She has also travelled to Guatemala with Pencils of Promise, where she visited schools and supported efforts to expand educational opportunities for children. Culpo is also a global ambassador for Pencils of Promise and Best Buddies International, an organisation that promotes inclusion for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Best Buddies describes its mission as addressing the social, physical and economic isolation experienced by the estimated 200 million people worldwide with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
Article Summary: Olivia Culpo launched More Than a Mask in May 2020 to raise funds for hunger relief. Each mask sold provided 100 meals to those in need. The initiative later funded more than 3 million meals through Feeding America. In a 2021 interview, Culpo credited her parents for her passion for philanthropy.

Article Title: An Ohio family farmed the same land for at least three generations; then a pipeline linked to Meta’s data center was mapped across 40 acres, but after the family challenged it, the developer chose ano
Article Text:
Representative image

For at least three generations, the Luidhardt family has farmed land north of Bowling Green, Ohio. That continuity came under pressure when the family learned that a natural gas pipeline connected to Meta’s data centre in Middleton Township could cross roughly 40 acres of their soybean fields. After Jon and Ken Luidhardt challenged the proposed route through the Ohio Power Siting Board, the developer ultimately selected a different path, according to BG Independent News and The Cool Down.The dispute became a broader test of how farmland, family heritage, and private corporate development collide in the age of rapid data-centre expansion. While Williams, the pipeline company’s parent firm, says it never pursued or threatened eminent domain on the route submitted for review, the Luidhardts say a map showed the pipeline crossing their property and that they felt compelled to fight back.A farm with deep family rootsJon Luidhardt said the land has been in his family for at least three generations, and he wants future generations to continue farming it. “We want to continue a fourth and fifth generation of farming,” he told BG Independent News.The property lies near the corner of Haskins Road and Hannah Road, between Bowling Green and Haskins. Its value to the family was not only agricultural, but also personal, because it represented continuity, work, and a way of life passed down over decades.That history helps explain why the family rejected a financial offer to sell part of the acreage. Luidhardt said pipeline representatives offered what he described as an “insane amount of money,” with some offers reportedly reaching as much as $200,000 per acre, but he argued that money could not replace family history.A pipeline for Meta’s data centerWill-Power, a pipeline company connected to Williams, sought land for a natural gas pipeline intended to serve the Meta data centre being built in Middleton Township. The pipeline would support the Apollo power plant, a natural gas facility located east of the data centre. The Apollo plant was approved by the Ohio Power Siting Board in February under an expedited review process. It will operate “behind the meter,” meaning it will serve the electricity needs of the adjacent Meta data centre rather than being physically connected to the public power grid, as per the reports.Because the facility is dedicated to a single customer, the approval process did not include public hearings. That lack of broader public involvement became a central concern for opponents, who argued that the project was designed to benefit one private company rather than the wider community.The family’s legal challengeThe reports further suggested that when Jon Luidhardt saw a map indicating that the pipeline would cross the family’s soybean field, he and his father contacted attorney Maurice Thompson, executive director of the 1851 Center for Constitutional Law in Columbus. The family had previously worked with Thompson to stop another pipeline from crossing their land. Thompson filed a motion to intervene with the Ohio Power Siting Board. He argued that private property in Ohio should not be taken simply to benefit a purely private corporate project, including a private pipeline built to fuel that project.The legal argument focused on eminent domain, the government power to take private property for public use. Thompson contended that the Apollo pipeline was solely intended to fuel Meta, rather than to heat Ohio homes or fuel vehicles, and therefore did not meet the traditional public-use standard.The developer says it chose another routeAfter the family’s challenge, Thompson said Will-Power informed regulators that the line would be redirected around Luidhardt Farms and removed from the family’s property. However, at the time of publication, the Luidhardts had not yet seen the revised map. Williams disputed the characterisation that eminent domain had been used or threatened. A company representative said the Luidhardt property was not on the route submitted for review and that the company had already achieved 100 percent acquisition before the farmer filed the intervention.The representative also said that all land options for the project involved voluntary agreements and that Williams did not pursue or threaten eminent domain against any landowner affected by the route. The company has previously described eminent domain as a last resort for pipeline projects.Why the case mattersThe dispute raises questions about whether state authority should be used to help a private corporation secure land for infrastructure that mainly benefits its own operations. Thompson argued that eminent domain is generally meant to serve a public use, not the needs of one private business.The case also reflects a wider tension between data-centre growth and rural communities. As companies build large facilities that require substantial electricity, water, and fuel infrastructure, nearby landowners may face pressure to sell or alter land that has been farmed for generations.There are environmental concerns as well. The pipeline would support a natural gas-powered facility for the data centre, potentially locking in additional polluting infrastructure as communities weigh the costs of rapid industrial expansion.What happens nextFor the Luidhardts, the reported reroute offers reassurance, but it does not fully close the issue. Jon Luidhardt said he wants to see the updated filing before treating the matter as resolved, and he also wanted the case tested in court.Thompson’s intervention did not produce a court ruling, but it appears to have contributed to the company’s decision to pursue a different route. He argued that public scrutiny can change corporate behaviour, saying that when the issue is highlighted, companies often find another way forward.The outcome is a partial victory for the family, but it also illustrates the uncertainty many landowners face when major infrastructure projects approach their property. A pipeline route can shift, offers can be substantial, and legal challenges may not always result in a formal ruling, yet they can still influence the final decision.A question of land, power, and progressThe Luidhardt case is ultimately about more than one pipeline or one data centre. It asks whether long-standing family farms should be preserved when a private development promises economic growth but requires land that families have cultivated for generations.Meta and its pipeline affiliates remain free to buy land from willing sellers. The dispute centred on whether a project serving a single private company should be able to rely on the power of eminent domain, or the threat of it, to overcome a landowner’s refusal.For now, the Luidhardt family’s land appears to be off the route. Their challenge shows how local opposition, legal intervention, and public attention can shape decisions about where large-scale infrastructure is placed, even in an era when data centres are expanding rapidly across the United States.
Article Summary: The Luidhardt family has farmed land north of Bowling Green, Ohio, for at least three generations. A natural gas pipeline connected to Meta’s data centre in Middleton Township could cross roughly 40 acres of their soybean fields. The Luidhardts say a map showed the pipeline crossing their property and that they felt compelled to fight back.

Article Title: Drone attack sinks ship off Bulgaria coast, second strike in a week
Article Text:
A drone assault near the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria led to one ship's sinking and damage to another.​

A drone attack sank a ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast on Tuesday, while another vessel was also hit, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.According to Reuters, the Maltese-flagged vessel Chelsea 3, which is owned by a Ukrainian company, was struck by three drones about 18 nautical miles off Bulgaria’s coast. All 15 crew members aboard the ship were rescued, while the second vessel sank in the attack.Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there was no clear evidence identifying those responsible for the attacks, describing the incident as the second of its kind in a week.“This is absolutely unacceptable — another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters,” Radev said, adding that he would speak with Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte.In an earlier incident on October 6, drones struck two merchant ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.The Togo-flagged cargo ship Alfa Watan sank, while the vessel Able, which was carrying grain, was damaged. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for that attack.Russia denied involvement in the attack, with its embassy in Sofia saying the merchant vessel Alfa Watan was not among the targets hit by Russian drones.The Russian defence ministry said the origin of the drones would need to be established through an investigation.The attacks have raised concerns over the security of commercial vessels operating near Bulgaria, a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato).The Black Sea remains a crucial route for grain and other commodities, particularly for Ukraine, and repeated strikes on merchant ships could disrupt maritime trade and increase risks for shipping operators.
Article Summary: Maltese-flagged vessel Chelsea 3, owned by a Ukrainian company, was struck by three drones about 18 nautical miles off Bulgaria’s coast. All 15 crew members aboard the ship were rescued, while the second vessel sank in the attack.

Article Title: Houthis target Saudi Aramco compound, limited fire reported
Article Text:
A missile attack targeted Saudi Aramco's administrative building, damaging upper floors of the headquarters complex (Reuters)

Saudi Aramco’s administrative building in Dhahran was hit in a missile attack that triggered a limited fire, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said on Wednesday, as the kingdom faced a fresh wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks.No casualties were reported in the incident, while Saudi authorities said they had intercepted missiles and drones targeting several parts of the country.A company source told Reuters that a ballistic missile struck the Aramco headquarters complex, damaging the top three floors of an office tower. The complex houses a major operations centre overseeing the state-owned oil giant’s network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.The energy ministry said authorities responded to the incident late on Tuesday and took the necessary measures.The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a missile over Dhahran, with fragments falling in a residential area. Authorities also reported intercepting and destroying missiles and drones targeting the capital, Riyadh, and Saudi Arabia’s southern region.In Riyadh, four people, including two women, a man and a child, were injured after fragments from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell in the capital, Saudi civil defense said on Wednesday. The debris also caused limited damage to 15 homes, a civil defense spokesperson said.The latest attacks follow a series of Houthi strikes on Saudi targets over the past week. Riyadh’s international airport has faced four strikes, including a ballistic missile attack on Saturday that killed 13 people.
Article Summary: Saudi Aramco's administrative building in Dhahran was hit in a missile attack that triggered a limited fire. No casualties were reported in the incident, while Saudi authorities said they had intercepted missiles and drones targeting several parts of the country. The latest attacks follow a series of Houthi strikes on Saudi targets over the past week.

Article Title: UK PM says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote, warns Europe faces same threat
Article Text: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accused Russia of interfering in Britain's 2016 vote to leave the European Union, warning that countries across Europe face the same threat.In excerpts from an episode of “The Rest Is Politics” podcast released on Sunday, Burnham said he asked his advisers after becoming prime minister in July whether Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum.“I've had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said.“These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he added.Burnham's remarks come amid warnings from UK intelligence agencies about the growing threat of Russian interference in Britain's democratic institutions. His comments are believed to mark the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the Brexit vote.Burnham also said he discussed possible links between Russia and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz when the two leaders met in Berlin last week.“You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe,” Burnham said.“There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” he added.In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee found that the British government had failed to fully assess the potential impact of Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts on the EU referendum.
Article Summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accused Russia of interfering in Britain's 2016 vote to leave the European Union. His comments are believed to mark the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the vote. Burnham also said he discussed possible links between Russia and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party.

Article Title: ‘Ties can’t hinge on one individual’: Hasina criticises Bangladesh’s Brics boycott
Article Text:
‘Deeply unfortunate’: Hasina on Bangladesh skipping Brics summit

Former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina has called Dhaka's decision to skip the Brics summit in India “deeply unfortunate”, saying the country's participation could have opened new opportunities for its economic and social development.“Foreign policy cannot be conducted through personal reaction or short-term political calculation,” Hasina told PTI, commenting on Bangladesh's absence from the summit.'Relations between two countries can't be determined by personal considerations or political sensitivities involving one individual,' she added.She also said Bangladesh was facing a serious national crisis, adding that “Bangladesh is passing through a grave national crisis and democratic space has been closed. Bangladesh needs a mature, balanced and confident foreign policy. A responsible government should open doors for the country, not close them."Meanwhile, the Indian government has reiterated that it invited Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to attend the BRICS summit as chair of BIMSTEC and also extended a separate invitation for a bilateral visit.In a letter dated July 14, accessed by TOI, Prime Minister Narendra Modi had invited Rahman to the summit in his capacity as BIMSTEC chair, saying his participation would “greatly enrich the deliberations”.Modi also noted that the summit was of special significance as it marked 20 years since the formal establishment of Brics.After Rahman was sworn in as prime minister, Modi invited him for a bilateral visit. However, Dhaka subsequently withdrew from talks to finalise the dates, apparently due to the lack of a firm commitment from India on the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.The ministry of external affairs (MEA) was responding to Dhaka's claim that the invitation for the summit had been extended to the BIMSTEC chair and not Rahman.“I have said this before as well, we had invited the PM of Bangladesh on a bilateral visit. Subsequently, he was invited for Brics summit as chair of Bimstec. So, he had received two invitations, one on the bilateral side and the other for Brics,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina says Bangladesh's decision to skip the Brics summit in India is 'deeply unfortunate' She says the country's participation could have opened new opportunities for its economic and social development. India has reiterated that it invited Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman to attend the BRICS summit as chair of BIMSTEC.

Article Title: Viola Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island; now she and husband Julius Tennon are donating $1.2 million to help local families
Article Text:
PC: Rhode Island Monthly

A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s mother

From a childhood in poverty to giving back to her Rhode Island roots

What families will be able to access at the new centre

How the new centre will support thousands of Rhode Island residents

For Viola Davis, the place where she grew up remains part of her story, even after a career that has taken her from Rhode Island to Hollywood. The award-winning actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a $1.2 million investment in Central Falls, the Rhode Island community where Davis once lived. The money will fund a new family engagement centre named after her mother, Mary Alice Davis, whose influence Davis has spoken about in explaining the project. Planned as a permanent base for local services, the centre will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center is being developed through the couple’s Davis-Tennon Foundation. Its purpose is to give residents a place to find practical support, whether they need help feeding their families, accessing educational opportunities or preparing for work.For Davis, naming the facility after her mother gives the project a personal connection. She has described the decision as a way of honouring a woman who continued to believe in people through difficult circumstances. The centre, she said, would carry that spirit forward by supporting individuals and creating opportunities for families.As reported by WJAR, the $1.2 million investment was announced on Monday, 20 July 2026. Rather than funding a single short-term initiative, the donation is intended to establish a lasting community resource in Central Falls, a city closely connected to Davis’s childhood.Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island, an experience that forms an important part of her personal history. She went on to build a career in film, television and theatre, becoming one of the most widely recognised actors of her generation. Her professional achievements have included major industry awards, but her latest investment focuses on a community far removed from the entertainment business.Central Falls was part of the environment in which Davis spent her early years. The new centre offers a way for her and Tennon to direct resources towards residents who may face financial pressures and limited access to services.The couple's contribution is being made through their foundation, which has an existing connection to Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry already serves about 3,000 people each month. The new facility is expected to provide a broader base for that work, alongside services aimed at parents, adults seeking new skills and families looking for guidance.Tennon, who is originally from Austin, Texas, has also expressed his commitment to supporting Rhode Island. Although the state is not his birthplace, he and Davis are directing the investment towards a community that holds particular significance for his wife.The planned facility will bring several services together in one location. These include a parent resource centre, a parent university and adult empowerment programmes, giving parents and other residents access to information and opportunities for learning.Food assistance will remain part of the work. The expanded Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry is expected to build on a service that already reaches thousands of people monthly. The centre will also provide workforce development and financial literacy programmes, along with family engagement activities, educational workshops and community events.For people looking for help with more than one issue, having these services in the same place could make it easier to find the right support. Someone visiting for food assistance, for example, may also be able to access parenting resources or information about employment training.The facility will also serve as the permanent administrative headquarters of the Davis-Tennon Foundation. This gives the organisation a local base from which to coordinate its activities and maintain its work in the area.Angelo Garcia, chair of the foundation, said, "Whether someone comes seeking food, parenting resources, educational support, workforce training, or guidance through a difficult season, our goal is simple: one place where people are welcomed, connected, and empowered.”The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry provides an established starting point for the project. Its reported monthly reach of around 3,000 individuals gives an indication of the demand for food assistance in the community and the role the new centre could play in extending that support.The planned expansion will place the pantry within a wider network of family and adult services. Residents will have access not only to food assistance but also to programmes intended to support education, financial understanding and employment prospects.The centre's effectiveness will depend on how these services are delivered and how well they meet local needs once the facility is operating. The announcement sets out the intended range of programmes, although it does not specify an opening date or provide a detailed timetable for their introduction.By combining food assistance with educational, parenting and employment services, the centre aims to address several practical challenges faced by families in one location.The project also extends the Davis-Tennon Foundation’s existing work in Rhode Island, with the new facility intended to provide a permanent base for its community programmes in Central Falls.
Article Summary: A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s mother. The actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a new family engagement centre in Central Falls, Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.

Article Title: Yunus called ‘terrorist’ by Awami backers at US airport
Article Text: DHAKA: Nobel laureate and former Bangladesh interim govt chief adviser Muhammad Yunus was confronted by a group of Awami League supporters at New York’s John F Kennedy airport, who termed him a “terrorist” for “killing civilians, arresting thousands and destroying democracy in Bangladesh”.Bangladesh govt condemned the harassment of the former chief adviser, while the PM’s information and broadcasting adviser Zahed Ur Ra­hman said govt views the incident — a video of which has surfaced online — as “Awami terror” and necessary action will be taken.The foreign ministry said it has asked its mission in NY to take up the matter with law enforcement agencies. “You killed a thousand people in Bangladesh. You terrorist! Why did you come here? Why did you arrest 2,00,000 people?... He (Yunus) killed a thousand police in my country. He destroyed democracy,” a supporter of the pa­r­ty, was heard saying as a wheelchair-bound Yunus was leav­ing the airport Monday.

Article Title: William Shatner underwent kidney stone removal; the stone was later auctioned for $75,000, with the money helping a Louisiana family get home
Article Text:
An offer William Shatner couldn't quite refuse

The kidney stone became an unlikely publicity stunt

How the money helped a family in Louisiana

Most people who pass a kidney stone would happily never see it again, but William Shatner’s experience took an unexpected turn. The Star Trek actor’s small black kidney stone, which he assumed had been discarded after removal, became an unusual fundraising item when a Canadian gambling company expressed interest in buying it. The stone was eventually auctioned for $75,000. Combined with a contribution from his Boston Legal co-stars, the proceeds helped provide a home in Louisiana for a family of five. Nearly two decades later, Shatner revisited the story on Dropping Names ...and other things with Brent & Jonny, hosted by fellow Star Trek actors Brent Spiner and Jonathan Frakes. The episode was released on October 7, 2026.The company behind the unusual proposal was GoldenPalace.com, an online casino known for acquiring bizarre objects as publicity stunts. Its collection reportedly included a partially eaten cheese sandwich said to resemble the Virgin Mary.When the casino approached Shatner, he checked with his doctor to see whether the kidney stone had been retained. Fortunately, it had. What had once been a painful medical problem now offered an unexpected opportunity to raise money for charity.According to accounts of the 2006 transaction, the casino initially offered $15,000, which Shatner declined.The offer subsequently rose to $25,000. Recognising the publicity potential of the deal, Shatner sought $75,000, and the company agreed. The stone was later auctioned through Julien's Auctions in Los Angeles.The fundraising effort also involved his Boston Legal co-stars. Shatner recalled their contribution as $25,000 during his recent podcast appearance, although his account in 2006 put the figure at $20,000. Depending on which account is used, the combined total was either $100,000 or $95,000.Shatner found humour in the unusual transaction, joking about the stone's size and the idea of turning it into jewellery. His willingness to laugh at himself helped make the story memorable, while the charitable purpose gave the sale significance beyond its novelty.For GoldenPalace.com, the purchase offered an unconventional way to attract attention. Shatner explained that the company faced restrictions on conventional advertising and was looking for alternative ways to generate publicity. Buying a celebrity's kidney stone provided a distinctive story that attracted media coverage.The company reportedly planned to display the stone on tour, turning the medical curiosity into a promotional attraction. Meanwhile, the sale became part of a wider effort to support affordable housing.The money raised through the auction and the cast's contribution went to Habitat for Humanity, a non-profit organisation that helps people access safe and affordable housing. Shatner said the funds helped provide a home in Louisiana for a family of five.Recalling the outcome on the podcast, the actor said he believed the family was still living in the house the last time he checked. His account brought the story back to its central purpose: using an unusual fundraising opportunity to help people secure a place to live.The initiative brought together the casino's publicity ambitions, Shatner's willingness to part with an unusual personal possession and his co-stars' support for the cause. Together, their contributions helped turn an extraordinary auction into practical housing assistance.The sale took place while Shatner was starring in Boston Legal, which ran from 2004 to 2008. He played attorney Denny Crane alongside James Spader, who portrayed Alan Shore. The series combined courtroom drama with comedy and became another notable chapter in Shatner's long career.
Article Summary: William Shatner's kidney stone was auctioned for $75,000 in 2006. The proceeds helped provide a home in Louisiana for a family of five. The Star Trek actor revisited the story on Dropping Names...and other things with Brent & Jonny.

Article Title: Two Arizona brothers, aged 10 and 12, vanished into the desert; trackers followed more than 6 miles of footprints before a helicopter-assisted search found them safe after eight hours
Article Text: Everyone's childhood often contains memories where they entered into some dangerous territories only to be saved by their parents. Often, when one is with their siblings or friends, they end up disregarding the path and are more focused on the company, which can sometimes lead them astray. This is what happened with two young brothers who vanished into the Arizona desert, only to be rescued after a helicopter-assisted search.12-year-old Atom Ward and 10-year-old Jack Ward had vanished when they were playing outside. The officials received a call from a father on October 11, Sunday, reporting he couldn't find his two children who were playing outside, the Mohave County Sheriff's Office said in an alert. At the same time, officials began the search for the two brothers who were last seen by their dad leaving their home on foot in the 1000 block of Birdle Lane in Mohave Valley earlier that afternoon, just before 4 pm.He began tracking his children, including Jack, who happened to be barefoot, said the officials. The family also began searching the surrounding areas and contacting local businesses to determine if the boys had stopped by.After rescue teams arrived, they began a "route and location search", the sheriff's office said. "Trackers confirmed the tracks being followed by the father were the kids' tracks and tracking teams continued following them," the department added.A rescue helicopter from the Arizona Department of Public Safety was dispatched from Phoenix while the Mohave County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue took over the trail, along with a K-9 Mano with the search and rescue team were aso deployed in the extensive search efforts. By midnight, the little duo was found walking near Spirit Mountain Casino in Mohave Valley, over six miles from their home.“Family met them at that location and brought them back home,” officials said. “They were in good health and the 10-year-old child was still barefoot.”However, it still remains unclear why the children ventured away from home in the first place. For the family and rescuers, the end of the search was a moment to celebrate. “Great job by everyone!” the sheriff’s office said.
Article Summary: Atom Ward, 12, and Jack Ward, 10, were last seen by their dad leaving their home in Mohave Valley, Arizona, on October 11, just before 4 pm. He began tracking his children, including Jack, who happened to be barefoot. A rescue helicopter from the Arizona Department of Public Safety was dispatched from Phoenix while the Mohave County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue took over the trail. By midnight, the little duo was found walking near Spirit Mountain Casino, over six miles from their home.

Article Title: Young Jain Professionals convention blends Silicon Valley innovation with Jain values
Article Text:
The convention brought together participants to explore innovation, networking & Jain philosophy. (Photo credit: Zak Khokhar / The American Bazaar)

MILPITAS, California:

Technology and

entrepreneurship

Professional development and Jain philosophy

Cultural celebrations

Plant-based dining

(Jayujyoti Mullik contributed to this report. By arrangement with

)

More than 300 people, including spiritual leaders, technology executives, entrepreneurs, investors and young professionals, attended the four-day Young Jain Professionals (YJP) Convention 2026, which concluded here on October 12.Held at the Embassy Suites under the theme “Reinventing Your Wheel,” the convention brought together participants to explore innovation, career development, networking and Jain philosophy. The program featured keynote addresses, technology discussions, professional development workshops, cultural performances and a startup pitch competition, according to the official program guide.YJP is an initiative of the Federation of Jain Associations in North America (JAINA), an umbrella organization dedicated to preserving, practicing and promoting Jain religious values and the Jain way of life.The gathering drew prominent speakers from the fields of philanthropy, technology and investment, including Dr. Jasvant Modi, a leading Jain philanthropist and driving force behind the establishment of Jain academic chairs worldwide; Kanwal Rekhi, a pioneering Silicon Valley investor; Arvind Jain, founder and CEO of Glean; Rajen Sheth, chairman of Boardwalk Development Group; and Deep Nishar, former managing director at General Catalyst.Jain spiritual leaders, including Rushiji Hem Vijay Maharaj and Dr. Arun Vijay Maharaj, also addressed the gathering, underscoring the convention’s emphasis on integrating professional growth with Jain spiritual traditions and principles.Sunny Jain, a project manager at Goldman Sachs in Dallas, described the convention as an opportunity for Jain professionals from across the United States and Canada to connect, exchange ideas and support one another’s professional growth.“[It] has been an incredible forum to bring Jains across the nation United States and Canada to come together in a place where we can connect with like-minded people, learn about Jain values, connect on a professional level, how can we leverage mentorship, leverage our contact and be able to help each other grow in this community,” he said.Jain, who served on the organization’s board in 2018 and 2019, told The American Bazaar that the convention offered valuable opportunities to learn from accomplished members of the community.He said he attended “some incredible session” and listened “to some great leaders and speakers in our community that have succeeded and are willing to share that wisdom with others in our community.”Technology and innovation figured prominently in the convention’s program, reflecting the growing influence of Jain professionals in Silicon Valley and other technology hubs.A panel titled “TECHnically Speaking” explored emerging trends and developments in the technology sector. Panelists included Anand Oswal, executive vice president and general manager of AI and network security at Palo Alto Networks; Lavina Kavediya, a product leader specializing in consumer AI and retail technology; and Dr. Nikunj Mehta, founder and CEO of Falkonry.The discussion covered a range of topics, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, consumer technology, industrial Internet of Things (IoT) applications and machine learning.Entrepreneurship was another major focus, highlighted by the YJP Shark Tank pitch competition on Oct. 11. The top three winners received cash prizes of $5,001, $2,501 and $1,501, respectively.Prithvion, founded by plant scientist Aishwarya Kothari, won the competition. The company is developing a biology-aware disease prediction platform that forecasts fungal disease risk up to seven days before symptoms appear. By integrating pathogen kinetics, host crop phenology and hyperlocal microclimate data, the platform aims to help growers determine when the risk of disease warrants spraying and when treatment can be skipped.Kothari, who has a background in synthetic biology and cellular agriculture, founded Prithvion to address the gap between growers’ needs and the capabilities of generic agricultural technology tools.The judging panel included Sahil Kothari, an entrepreneur, investor and mentor; Mansi Shah, a law partner and technology investor; Deep Nishar; Pranjal Daga, founder of Accend and a participant in Y Combinator’s Summer 2023 cohort; and Priyanka Shah, a life sciences portfolio lead and venture adviser.Beyond technology and entrepreneurship, the convention placed considerable emphasis on personal growth and professional development, with two sets of breakout sessions designed to encourage participants to reflect on their careers and broaden their perspectives.The Oct. 10 workshop, titled “Re-Calibrating…,” explored Jain philosophical concepts such as karma and rebirth, alongside topics including creative expression, personal identity, confidence and improvisation. The sessions sought to connect philosophical reflection with professional and personal development.A second workshop, “Circling Back Forward,” held on October 11, covered a wide range of topics, from agentic and physical AI to venture capital, decision-making and Ayurveda.One session examined Anekantavada, the Jain principle of multiple perspectives, and how it could be applied to identifying investment opportunities in venture capital.Other sessions explored what makes startups attractive to investors and how Jain values can guide decisions involving business strategy and environmental impact.The program also included a structured networking initiative titled “Chain Reaction,” designed to connect attendees with potential mentors and industry leaders through guided discussions and speed-networking sessions.Alongside its professional development sessions, the convention offered cultural and social events that brought participants together outside formal discussions.The opening evening featured “Pacific Coast Hungama,” a talent show showcasing music and entertainment. Saturday’s festivities included “Raas in the Redwoods,” a Garba Night celebration, while the closing evening featured the “Golden State Gala.”Shikha Kothari, an adviser to Young Jain Professionals, highlighted the diversity of talent on display.“It’s very cool to see the people who are poets, we had from different angles, and we had some beautiful classical pieces, [and] we had fusion pieces,” she said.Featured performers included Jai Loonker, a dancer, choreographer and engineer, and Priya Puram, an Indian American stand-up comedian and product manager based in San Francisco.For Apeksha Shah, an Orange, California, resident who immigrated to the United States from Godhra, Gujarat, Garba Night was among the convention’s highlights.“It was very amazing,” she said.Shah particularly enjoyed the opportunity to celebrate with participants who had come from different parts of India, including Mumbai and Gujarat.Food was another highlight of the convention, which served a plant-based Jain menu throughout the four days, offering participants a variety of Indian and international dishes.The selections included poha and chia pudding for breakfast, a Mexican-themed lunch, an Indo-Chinese dinner, pani puri, corn chaat, Mediterranean falafel and Thai cuisine.Priyanka Chordia, founder of D’Deco Jewels, who oversaw the planning and coordination of more than 13 meals and snacks during the convention, said the organizers wanted to use the event to promote greater awareness of vegan food.“Last year we had decided that, in our convention, we will emphasize the importance of vegan food along with Jain food,” she said.“Through this journey, we realized that many people are not aware of veganism and how to prepare vegan food at home. Through the convention, our aim was to not only feed people but to raise awareness that you can do all cuisines and all dishes vegan.”Chordia, who is based in New York, said coordinating the food arrangements for a convention in the San Francisco Bay Area presented logistical challenges. However, working with Hasmukh and Kavita Patel of Utsav Kitchen, the team managed to serve 13 meals over four days without repeating dishes.The menu spanned Indian, Mexican, Mediterranean, Indo-Chinese and Thai cuisines, along with a wide selection of desserts, including vegan falooda.For Sunny Jain, a Dallas resident, the food was among the most memorable aspects of the gathering.“My highlights have been the food,” he said. “I think the food has been absolutely incredible. It’s been a you know fully plant-based and you know being able to eat everything and it’s been absolutely delicious.”The convention concluded on October 12 with a closing ceremony and lunch, followed by a visit to the Jain Center of Northern California.
Article Summary: More than 300 people attended the Young Jain Professionals (YJP) Convention 2026. The convention brought together participants to explore innovation, career development, networking and Jain philosophy. The program featured keynote addresses, technology discussions, professional development workshops, cultural performances and a startup pitch competition.

Article Title: A rare Ten Commandments tablet was reportedly used as a paving stone for decades; it sold for $5.04 million despite doubts over its origins
Article Text:
PC: AP News

How was the rare Ten Commandments tablet discovered in 1913

How did the Ten Commandments tablet reach Sotheby’s auction

Why have experts questioned the authenticity of the tablet

How does the tablet differ from the traditional version

How much did the tablet sell for at Sotheby’s auction

A rare stone tablet inscribed with the Ten Commandments sold for $5.04 million at a Sotheby’s auction in New York on 18 December 2024, decades after it was reportedly used as a paving stone. According to The New York Times, the tablet was discovered during railway construction near the coast of what is now southern Israel in 1913, but its historical significance was not recognised immediately. Sotheby’s dated the 115-pound artefact to the late Roman-Byzantine period, around 1,500 years ago. However, experts questioned its provenance and authenticity because its discovery lacked independently verifiable archaeological documentation.The tablet’s discovery dates back to 1913, when a railway was being built near the coast of what is now southern Israel. Jacob Kaplan, who later investigated the stone, reported that it had been found during the construction work. Rather than being immediately recognised as an important historical artefact, the inscribed stone was reportedly used as a paving stone at a nearby home, with its inscription facing upwards as it was set into the ground.Kaplan published his findings in 1947 in The Bulletin of the Jewish Palestine Exploration Society, a scholarly journal. He died in 1989. The account of the discovery subsequently became part of the tablet’s documented history, although experts later questioned whether the reported circumstances could be independently verified. The absence of archaeological excavation records from 1913 became a central issue in discussions about the stone’s authenticity.The tablet eventually entered the antiquities market. It reached an Israeli antiquities dealer in 1995 before being acquired by the Living Torah Museum in Brooklyn. In 2016, collector Mitchell S. Cappell purchased it for $850,000. Cappell later consigned the stone to Sotheby’s, where it was auctioned in December 2024.Sotheby’s described the tablet as approximately 1,500 years old and associated it with the late Roman-Byzantine period. The stone weighs 115 pounds, measures two feet in length and bears an inscription in Paleo-Hebrew, an early form of Hebrew writing. The auction house cited the lettering, wear and weathering as evidence relevant to determining its age. Selby Kiffer, Sotheby’s international senior specialist for books and manuscripts, highlighted the importance of the script, stating, “The script is a key to it. We know when it went out of common usage.”Despite Sotheby’s claims about the tablet’s age and significance, specialists raised concerns about its provenance, meaning the documented history of an object’s ownership and discovery. Patty Gerstenblith, director of the Centre for Art, Museum and Cultural Heritage Law at DePaul University College of Law, described the auction result as “remarkable” but emphasised that doubts about the artefact needed serious consideration.In an email quoted by The New York Times, Gerstenblith said, “The inscription has no objectively verifiable origin, such as discovery during a documented archaeological excavation.” She also questioned aspects of the discovery account, noting that “Several elements of the story, such as that its significance was unrecognised for several decades, seem to stretch belief.” Her concerns centred on the lack of independently verifiable archaeological evidence establishing when and where the tablet was originally found.Brian I. Daniels, director of research and programmes at the Penn Cultural Heritage Centre in Philadelphia, also highlighted the risks associated with antiquities from the region. He said, “Objects from this region of the world are rife with fakes.” However, he acknowledged that the tablet could still prove genuine, adding, “Maybe it’s absolutely authentic, and this truly is a historic find.”Christopher A. Rollston, chairman of the Department of Classical and Near Eastern Languages and Civilisations at George Washington University, questioned whether the stone could reliably be dated to the late Roman-Byzantine period. He said that it was possible the tablet had been carved closer to the time of its reported discovery, rather than centuries earlier. “But there is no way that this can be known,” Rollston said in an email quoted by The New York Times. He added, “After all, these were not found on an archaeological excavation. We don’t even know who actually found them.”Rollston also challenged the account that the tablet had been used as a paving stone after its discovery in 1913. He pointed to the absence of contemporary records and the possibility that stories about an object's discovery could be fabricated to make it appear more authentic. “The problem is that we have zero documentation from 1913, and since pillagers and forgers often concoct such stories to give an inscription an aura of authenticity, this story could actually just be a tall tale told by a forger or some antiquities dealer,” he said.The tablet contains a version of the Ten Commandments that differs in certain respects from the wording commonly known today. It omits the prohibition against taking the Lord’s name in vain and includes an instruction to worship on Mount Gerizim, a sacred site for the Samaritans in what is now the West Bank.Rollston specifically questioned the inclusion of the Mount Gerizim directive, suggesting that unusual details can sometimes be introduced into forged inscriptions to attract interest. He said, “Forgers during the past 150 years, when they fabricate their forgeries, often throw in surprising content.” He added, “And they do this to garner more interest in their forgery.” These concerns formed part of the wider debate over whether the tablet’s inscription reflected an ancient religious tradition or a later fabrication.Sotheby’s, meanwhile, defended the research conducted on the artefact. Sharon Liberman Mintz, the auction house’s international senior specialist in Judaica, books and manuscripts, said the tablet had been “widely studied, researched, and published by the world’s leading scholars.” She described its significance as undisputed and welcomed the prospect of it being preserved in an Israeli institution. The Israel Antiquities Authority was also pleased that the artefact would return to Israel.The anonymous buyer who purchased the tablet at Sotheby’s planned to donate it to an Israeli institution, according to the auction house. Sotheby’s said the artefact would have a home where it could be preserved and continue to be studied. Its sale followed more than 10 minutes of bidding and exceeded the auction house’s original estimate of $1 million to $2 million.The auction established the price paid for the tablet, but the questions surrounding its origins remained a separate matter. While Sotheby’s presented it as an exceptionally significant religious artefact and cited its inscription, physical condition and scholarly research, experts highlighted the lack of independently documented archaeological evidence. The stone’s journey from its reported use as a paving stone to a multimillion-dollar auction therefore remains closely linked to both its historical claims and the continuing debate over its authenticity.
Article Summary: The 115-pound artefact was discovered near the coast of what is now southern Israel in 1913. It was reportedly used as a paving stone at a nearby home. Sotheby’s dated the tablet to the late Roman-Byzantine period, around 1,500 years ago. Experts questioned its provenance and authenticity because its discovery lacked independently verifiable archaeological documentation.

Article Title: An 18-year-old used 3D printers to build a shoe-accessories brand before launching a viral beer koozie that made $315,000 in one month
Article Text:
Image: Solefully/Michael Satterlee

How an 18-year-old used spare 3D printers from his shoe accessories brand Solefully to start a new business

How Satterlee designed the Beerzooka, a patent-pending beer koozie, and prototyped it in a single day

His shoe accessories brand Solefully (Image: Solefully)

How social media, Facebook ads, and viral videos drove Cruise Cup from $100,000 to $315,000 in monthly sales

Why Satterlee wants to manufacture the Beerzooka in metal and urges young entrepreneurs to test every idea

Most teenagers spend high school juggling homework and weekend plans, but Michael Satterlee spent his building a business powered by 3D printers. What began as a shoe accessories brand became the launchpad for something much bigger, a viral beer koozie that generated more than $300,000 in a single month. His story shows how social media, inexpensive technology, and constant experimentation can help a young founder test ideas without risking much money. It also reveals the lessons that come with fast growth, from hiring help to keeping up with demand. Here is how spare 3D printers became a real business.Michael Satterlee, 18, of Clifton Park, New York, was a full-time high school student when he ran Solefully, a six-figure business that designs and 3D prints unique accessories for Crocs, according to Entrepreneur, which told his story in an as-told-to format. Satterlee told Entrepreneur that he had a bunch of 3D printers from his time working on Solefully and was not using all of them because demand at the time was limited. He asked himself why he did not simply create a different e-commerce store to put those machines to work. After brainstorming, beer koozies, the insulating sleeves that keep a can cold, caught his eye. He wondered how he could make the product better and, more importantly, how he could make it go viral.His first question was how to make a koozie easier to use. His answer was a design that opens on both the top and the bottom, so cans slide in easily. He then tested ideas for making the product go viral and found that raising the cap slightly makes the can eject when a new one is loaded, much like a shell reloading mechanism. Because he has a lot of experience with computer-aided design, he told Entrepreneur he had a working product within a day, after a couple of printed variations. The product became the Beerzooka; it is a patent-pending creation from his company, Cruise Cup. Satterlee said he has patents and trademarks filed to protect it.He carried lessons from his first business into Cruise Cup, including how to structure a product on social media and build a Shopify store. When he posted the Beerzooka online, it drew 50 million views. Cruise Cup launched in August 2025 with about $100,000 in sales that first month, he said. Sales dipped to about $55,000 in September when he began Facebook ads, but organic views weakened. Ramping up paid ads in October brought sales back to $100,000, and November reached $315,000. He told Entrepreneur he tests content on TikTok and Instagram first, and if it works there, it will work on Facebook ads 90 per cent of the time. In December, he cut ad spend entirely to fulfil holiday orders.A build plate of three Beerzookas takes 15 hours to print, so he needs many printers, and even with 150 machines, a maximum of 400 cups per day can leave a backlog when a video goes viral.
